blocks.text: **Hip osteoarthritis (hip OA)** is a long-term condition of the hip ball-and-socket joint in which the cartilage thins and the bone and surrounding tissues change. It causes pain, stiffness and loss of function, and it is a common reason for walking difficulty in older adults [Ref - to verify]. Risk factors include age, previous hip injury or childhood hip disorders, shape differences of the hip, and heavy physical work [Ref - to verify].
OA is a whole-joint condition. X-ray changes do not always match pain or function, so treatment is guided by symptoms and function, not images alone [Ref - to verify].

items: Pain in the groin or front of the hip, often spreading to the front of the thigh or the knee. Some people feel pain in the buttock or the side of the hip.
Pain with weight-bearing, walking, stairs, getting in and out of cars and putting on socks or shoes.
Short morning stiffness, stiffness after rest, and reduced hip movement, especially internal rotation and flexion.
A limp, and sometimes night pain in more advanced disease.
Often over 50 years old, or younger with a past hip problem [Ref - to verify].

blocks.text: Hip pain can be felt in the knee only, so always examine the hip when a patient has unexplained knee pain.

rows: Where is the pain: groin, side of hip, buttock, thigh or knee?
Intra-articular pain is usually groin or front hip
What makes it worse: walking, stairs, putting on shoes, getting up from a chair?
Under about 30 to 60 minutes supports OA [Ref - to verify]
Any childhood hip problems, injury or surgery?
Any night pain, rest pain or rapid worsening?
Any back pain or leg symptoms below the knee?
Steroid use, heavy alcohol, sickle cell disease?
What do you need to do?

items: Observe gait (limp, Trendelenburg pattern), posture and muscle wasting.
Hip range of movement, passive and active: flexion, internal rotation, external rotation, abduction, extension. Compare sides.
Special tests (Section E).
Strength of the hip abductors, extensors and flexors.
Thomas test for hip flexion contracture.
Lumbar spine and knee screen, and neurological screen.
Functional tests (chair stand, walking).

blocks.text: Honest note: no single test confirms hip OA. Limited range with pain, a typical history and X-ray changes support the diagnosis. Hip tests that reproduce pain show the joint is irritable but do not name the cause [Ref - to verify].
E1. Passive internal rotation

rows: Check for the early loss of internal rotation, a common sign of hip OA
Supine with the hip and knee at 90 degrees of flexion, or prone with the knee bent to 90 degrees
Hold the lower leg and rotate it outward so the thigh rotates inward. Measure the angle (goniometer if available) and compare with the other side; note pain and end-feel
Reduced internal rotation with pain or a firm end-feel; some criteria use a value around 15 to 25 degrees or less [Ref - to verify exact cut-off]
Similar movement to the other side without pain
Hip joint involvement; reduced internal rotation supports OA
Normal range varies between people; compare with the other side
Pelvis rotating; knee position changes; not stabilising the pelvis

blocks.text: E2. FADIR test (flexion, adduction, internal rotation)

rows: Check whether the hip joint is irritable in a compressed position
Flex the hip to about 90 degrees, then adduct and internally rotate it. Hold and note pain
Reproduction of the familiar groin pain
A sensitive test for intra-articular hip problems, but not specific to OA, impingement or labral tears [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: E3. FABER (Patrick) test

rows: Supine, the test foot placed on the opposite knee (flexion, abduction, external rotation)
Gently press the bent knee downward and the opposite pelvis down
Groin pain (hip joint) or back pain near the sacroiliac joint (pelvic source). Record location
Not specific; also positive with muscle and joint problems [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: E4. Scour test

rows: Flex and adduct the hip to about 90 degrees; apply gentle compression down the thigh and move the hip in a small arc
Pain, catching or grinding in the hip

blocks.text: E5. Clinical cluster

A published cluster used several findings together (squat pain, painful active hip flexion, pain with scour test, painful active extension, reduced internal rotation). When most are present, hip OA is more likely [Ref - to verify exact criteria]. A negative cluster lowers the likelihood but does not exclude OA.
E6. Function and outcome measures
30-second chair stand, timed up and go, a walking test, and the Hip disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (HOOS) [Ref - to verify].

rows: Lateral hip pain, lying on that side, single-leg stance pain
Younger, groin pain with flexion and rotation, clicking
Sudden or severe groin pain, risk factors
Pain with impact, runners or low bone density
Inguinal hernia, adductor or other groin pain
Fever, severe pain, unable to move

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: After a fall: cannot bear weight, shortened and externally rotated leg, severe groin pain
Do not move the hip; emergency services
Hot swollen hip with fever, severe pain on any movement
Adolescent with hip, thigh or knee pain and a limp
Sudden severe groin pain, steroid use, alcohol, sickle cell
Pain with impact in a runner or older person with low bone density
Constant night pain, weight loss, cancer history
Saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.

Age 45 or over, activity-related groin or front hip pain, reduced internal rotation and flexion, no flags? **Yes:** working diagnosis is hip OA; imaging can confirm and is considered by a doctor when it will change management [Ref - to verify].
Lumbar or knee source more likely? Use that pathway.
Start education, exercise and function-based treatment.
If severe pain, major loss of function or no improvement after good non-surgical care: specialist review for injection or hip replacement.

rows: Hip mobilization (long-axis distraction, lateral and posterior glides)
May give short-term pain relief and range gains when added to exercise [Ref - to verify]
Stiff painful hip with reduced range
Supine, gentle grades, 30 to 60 seconds per technique

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** education and exercise. Manual therapy is an optional short-term adjunct, best combined with exercise. Do not claim that mobilization rebuilds cartilage or restores a normal joint space.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

blocks.text: **Principle:** exercise and education are first-line in major guidelines [Ref - to verify]. A mix of strengthening, range of motion and aerobic activity two to three times a week is common. Aquatic exercise is a good option when weight-bearing is painful.

rows: Lying with the knees bent, lift the hips
Lying on the side, lift the top leg
Hip flexor and adductor gentle stretch
Stationary cycling, walking or water exercise
10 to 20 minutes, 3 to 5 days a week

blocks.text: **Symptom rule:** pain during exercise of up to about 4 out of 10 that settles within 24 hours is generally acceptable [Ref - to verify]. A hot, swollen hip or a sudden severe pain is not.

**Weight management and aids:** if overweight, modest weight loss may reduce pain [Ref - to verify]. A walking stick held in the hand opposite the painful hip reduces load. Supportive shoes, a raised chair and a raised toilet seat can help function.

**Medical options (decided by doctors):** pain medication, corticosteroid injection for short-term relief, and total hip replacement for severe, persistent cases, which generally gives good results [Ref - to verify]. Rehabilitation before and after surgery follows the surgeon's protocol.

items: **Visit 1:** screen flags and the lumbar spine and knee, confirm the clinical diagnosis, explain OA in plain language, set a goal.
**Early:** reduce painful loading, start gentle range and strengthening, add aerobic activity.
**Middle:** progress strength and function; address weight, aids and footwear.
**Late:** self-management plan for flares and maintenance exercise.
**If limited progress:** specialist review for injection or surgery.

blocks.text: Record pain scale, HOOS, passive internal rotation and flexion, hip strength, 30-second chair stand, timed up and go, walking tolerance and the patient's goal.

rows: No improvement after about 6 to 12 weeks of regular exercise
Review dose, adherence and diagnosis; consider specialist input
Sudden severe pain, fever or inability to bear weight

blocks.text: **Case:** A 64-year-old woman has 2 years of groin pain spreading to the knee, worse on stairs and getting out of the car. Passive internal rotation is much reduced on the left with pain, and FADIR reproduces her groin pain. She walks with a mild limp. X-ray shows joint space narrowing. Lumbar examination is normal.

**Working diagnosis:** left hip osteoarthritis. **Plan:** education, strengthening and aerobic exercise (water exercise if painful), a stick in the right hand, footwear and chair advice, review in 4 to 6 weeks, and discuss specialist referral if function remains poor.
**Questions and answers**

items: Why examine the hip when a patient reports only knee pain? Hip pain is often felt in the knee, so a hip cause can be missed if only the knee is examined.
Why is FADIR not a diagnostic test for OA? It is sensitive but not specific, so a positive result shows an irritable hip joint and does not name the cause.
An adolescent has knee pain and a limp. What do you do? Suspect a hip cause, check hip rotation and refer urgently for slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
After a fall, an older patient has a shortened, externally rotated leg. What now? Suspect a hip fracture and call emergency services.
Why is exercise recommended even when the hip hurts? It improves pain, strength and function for many people and avoiding movement tends to worsen weakness and stiffness [Ref - to verify].
**Initial approach:** education, exercise and weight management when relevant.
**Justifying findings:** age, groin pain, reduced internal rotation, no flags.
**Priority:** strength, fitness and function.
**Manual therapy:** optional short-term adjunct with exercise.
**Exercise:** hip strengthening, range, aerobic activity, water exercise if needed.
**Modalities:** limited role.
**Tell the patient:** OA is manageable, movement helps, and surgery is an effective option if needed.
**Avoid:** prolonged rest, missing referral for urgent causes, promising a cure.
**Measure:** HOOS, internal rotation, chair stand, TUG, goal.
**If no improvement:** specialist review.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** self-management plan and maintenance exercise in place.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** adult, no fracture or infection, no inflammatory disease.

items: **Can be tested:** whether exercise, education and weight loss improve pain and function; whether adding manual therapy helps.
**Hypotheses:** that muscle strengthening reduces joint load.
**Future questions:** best exercise dose, and optimal timing of surgery.
